name: Datadog
summary: A hosted monitoring platform: an agent on every host ships metrics, logs and traces to Datadog’s SaaS, which bills per host, per GB and per metric.
intro: The Datadog Agent is an open-source program, written in Go, that runs on every host, or as one pod per node in Kubernetes. It runs checks against the machine and the software on it through more than 1,000 integrations, accepts custom metrics over DogStatsD on UDP port 8125, takes traces from Datadog’s tracing libraries on TCP port 8126 and OpenTelemetry data over OTLP on 4317 and 4318, and tails log files. It sends everything over HTTPS on port 443 to the Datadog site (region) your account lives in. Storage, dashboards, search, monitors and alerting all live in Datadog’s proprietary backend, so the Agent is the only part you run.

Each product has its own meter. Infrastructure Monitoring is billed per host per month ($15 Pro, $23 Enterprise, billed annually), with hosts counted every hour and billed at the high-water mark of the lowest 99% of those hours. APM adds $31 per host. Logs are billed twice: $0.10 per GB ingested, then $1.70 per million events indexed for 15-day search. Custom metrics are counted per unique combination of metric name and tag values, and each host includes only 100 (Pro) or 200 (Enterprise). RUM, security, on-call and other products are priced separately, so the bill depends on how many hosts, tags, log lines and products you use, not only on the plan.
strengths: Metrics, traces and logs in one product, joined by shared tags, so you can go from a latency graph to the traces and log lines behind it
More than 1,000 integrations with out-of-the-box dashboards for common databases, web servers and cloud services
Nothing to operate besides the Agent: Datadog runs storage and keeps full-resolution metrics for 15 months on paid plans
Speaks OpenTelemetry: OTLP into the Agent, its own DDOT Collector, or direct OTLP intake, so instrumentation stays vendor-neutral
Logs can be ingested, live-tailed and archived to your own S3 bucket without indexing them, so you pay to search only what you choose
limits: Many meters at once: hosts, GB ingested, million indexed log events, indexed spans and custom metrics. A tag with many values multiplies custom metrics, and every metric scraped from a Prometheus endpoint counts as custom
Extra indexed custom metrics are billed at a price set in your contract, not on the public price list, and installing the Agent inside each container makes each container a billable host
Proprietary SaaS with no self-hosted option. OpenTelemetry keeps instrumentation portable, but dashboards, monitors and saved queries don’t move to another tool
The free tier stops at 5 hosts and keeps metrics for only one day
OTLP log ingestion is off by default “to avoid unexpected billing”: a sign of how fast log volume turns into cost

story: Olivier Pomel and Alexis Lê-Quôc worked together at Wireless Generation, a New York education software company, Pomel as VP of Technology and Lê-Quôc running operations. Developers and operations teams, the company later argued, had worked apart with separate goals, priorities and tools. The two founded Datadog in New York in June 2010 with the goal, as the company later put it, of “breaking down silos between Dev and Ops”.

The first product, in 2012, was infrastructure monitoring built for cloud servers that come and go. APM followed in 2017, and in 2018 log management completed what Datadog called the “three pillars of observability”: metrics, traces and logs in one place. The 2018 log product split ingestion from indexing, so customers could collect and archive every log but pay to index only some. Datadog went public on the Nasdaq in September 2019 at $27 a share, under the ticker DDOG.
Since then the platform has grown into dozens of separately priced products, from real user monitoring and security to on-call and status pages, all fed by the same Agent and the same tags.

choices.choice: One agent per host, many integrations
choices.why: Cloud servers appear and disappear constantly. A single agent that discovers what runs on the host and reports it, rather than per-application setup, keeps monitoring up with that churn.
Metrics, traces and logs carry the same tags (host, service, env), which is what lets the product line them up side by side. It is also why each new tag value creates new billable custom metrics.
Indexing every log was too expensive, so teams dropped logs before sending them and lost them in incidents. Logging without Limits (2018) archives all logs cheaply and indexes only the ones you pick.
